old: Its old English-born name has vanished, pushed aside by a word borrowed from far away.
In some dialects, ordinary speakers misheard it and reshaped it into something involving a small bird.
That folk version, 'sparrowgrass,' still echoes in old country speech.
clues: This spring vegetable once had a homegrown Old English name meaning something like 'earth navel,' until a borrowed Greek word pushed it aside.
Its slender green spears with tight, scaly tips are sold in upright bundles, snapped at the woody end, then steamed or roasted; they are stalks, not pods like green beans.
Some English dialects reshaped its unfamiliar name into 'sparrowgrass,' and eating it famously gives urine a distinctive smell soon afterward.
